# Dialog policy

This page records the confirmation policy for leaving unfinished work and its relationship to the game's existing actions.

The current source contains no dialog component, native dialog element or leave-work handler. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly.

## The confirmation boundary

A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision.

There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved.

The policy does not define which future feature owns a leave route or a new navigation screen. Those boundaries have to be visible in the feature's actual code. The current page has no router and no alternate play screen. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers orientation when a feature introduces a main-area replacement.

## What the present controls actually do

`Controls.tsx` renders New Game and Restart as native buttons. Their callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. They do not consult `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before doing so. The existing game replaces immediately when those buttons are used.

BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation.

The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) documents the actual disclosure.

This distinction matters during incremental work. A new dialog in one feature does not silently change the semantics of every old control. When reading a change, follow the event handler to see whether it reaches a confirmation boundary, a parser, or the replacement directly. Similar visual labels do not establish the same lifecycle.

## Native behavior and application decisions

The policy names a native element because the interface already relies on browser semantics for buttons, forms, selects and details. A dialog has a different interaction boundary from an ordinary panel. Its opening, cancellation and closing need to be considered as a coherent interaction rather than a div painted over the board.

Using the element alone does not decide what leaving means for a game. The application still owns the transition that discards or replaces state. In the current implementation, that transition is represented by controller operations and `replaceGame`. Visual disappearance of an overlay is not evidence that a session was replaced, just as visual appearance is not evidence that play was paused.

The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.

No dialog state exists in `Session`. Its fields are `game`, `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. The existing `paused` flag specifically represents unfinished snapshot import. Reusing that flag for a new overlay without considering its other consumers would also affect Resume and load notices.

## Timing questions exposed by an overlay

A mismatch stores its remaining active milliseconds in game selection. The session clock advances it when the page is visible and the imported-pause flag is clear. Merely placing a dialog above the board is not one of those conditions in the current source.

Consequently, there is no existing rule here that opening a confirmation pauses the elapsed clock or mismatch. A feature implementation needs to be read for its actual timing behavior rather than assuming that every modal surface freezes play. [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) explain the established clock model.

Replacement does have a well-defined lifecycle today. `clock.reset()` and the session generation prevent old pending updates from affecting a replacement game. If a leave decision leads to that existing path, stale-timer protection still belongs to the session. The dialog does not need to know the two selected card indices to implement that protection.

The period between opening and making a decision is therefore worth observing in review. It can expose accidental differences between the visual state, current game state and timers. The observation is useful even when the feature's intended behavior is simply to preserve the current clock semantics.

## Focus ownership

Opening the confirmation establishes a temporary interaction context. The policy above states its initial focus and cancellation result. That avoids relying on DOM order alone to make the safe continuation choice the first keyboard target.

After a decision, the durability of the source control matters. Existing action buttons generally remain mounted after a deal replacement, while Resume removes itself. Game handles Resume by moving focus before the button is removed. That is a concrete example of a disappearing source, though it is not a dialog implementation.

A leave feature may keep or remove its trigger as part of its surrounding screen. Its focus return depends on which controls remain mounted. A review can inspect the final active element and its visibility.

The board also remembers focus independently of actual focus. Opening another surface would not, by itself, mean its last card index should become a selected turn. A player returning to the board still needs the distinction between orientation and activation described in [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md).

## Review notes for a proposed implementation

The most useful review evidence separates opening, continuing and leaving. A single screenshot of the open surface cannot establish which element is focused, whether Escape follows the continuation path, or whether the underlying controller already replaced the game before a decision.

A source trace can identify the first state-changing call relative to the decision. A keyboard trace can identify the active element at opening and after cancellation. A populated game, especially one with a pending mismatch, makes unintended early replacement visible. These are ways of observing the stated policy and existing game lifecycle, rather than additional product requirements.

Current browser tests establish focus retention on ordinary buttons, invalid draft preservation, Resume's transfer order and stale-timer protection. They do not establish a dialog journey. Any future report of dialog coverage has to point at the corresponding implementation and evidence, rather than citing those tests because they also involve focus.

The relevant background is [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) for element choice, [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) for page orientation and [New game and restart](../gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md) for the existing replacement boundary. Together they make it possible to review a concrete leave interaction alongside the existing game lifecycle.
# Focus policy

This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen.

Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things.

## Existing page and future screens

`Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen.

A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists.

The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus.

## Initial load is quiet

The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method.

The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board.

A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing.

## Deal actions retain their location

New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call.

The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms.

A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place.

Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows those cases in detail.

## Remembered board focus

Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`.

Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched.

Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) provides the calculations and edge behavior.

## Resume transfers before removal

Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target.

In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices.

The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment.

The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location.

## Visible focus and scroll clearance

`game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area.

The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail.

`useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible.

The helper leaves the outer page's scrolling to the browser. A review therefore measures both the card inside the board viewport and its visibility inside the window. A ring can be uncut by the board yet still sit partly below the window if the outer document did not move appropriately.

## Focus is not completion feedback

Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched.

Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched.

These examples are useful when evaluating a proposed effect that focuses something whenever `game` changes. Game changes for elapsed time, first reveals, turn results and resets. An effect tied to that broad object would combine very different events and could interrupt typing or navigation. The existing code places its explicit focus operations at narrower action boundaries.

## Review evidence

The keyboard browser check covers Tab exit, remembered re-entry and matched-card focus. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` covers Enter submission from Board code. `tests/focus-entry.e2e.test.ts` covers nearest alignment and the switch from pointer use to keyboard arrows. `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks outline clearance on large boards, including an interior card where container padding alone cannot protect the ring.

A useful focus report names the source control, action, destination and whether the source remains mounted. For example: “Enter in Board code loads 6x6, replaces the input and leaves Load board focused.” That is more precise than “load focuses correctly,” and it exposes why failure has a different result. [Interface review checklist](interface-review-checklist.md) gathers these journeys with layout and input checks.

For new screen work, the source review begins by locating the actual replacement boundary. For changes within the existing game page, it begins with the current action-specific behavior above. Screen replacement and the established board lifecycle have separate focus behavior.
# Target size policy

This page records the control target policy and explains the size constraints already present in the interface styles.

Target size is about the area a person can activate, not the size of a glyph drawn inside it. A card's marker is small, but the native button enclosing the whole card is the target. The same distinction applies to a summary's disclosure marker and the much larger summary row.

## Policy and present coverage

The existing code already gives cards a minimum track size and shared controls a minimum height. Extending the interface calls for checking the actual rendered target in the phone layout, where flex wrapping and available width matter. Every new control is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels at a 390 pixel wide viewport. This policy covers the rendered control area rather than enlarging only a decorative child or a focus ring.

The current styles are useful building blocks, but they are not proof of every dimension for an arbitrary new element. In particular, `.control` declares minimum height without a general minimum width. A new short-label action could be tall enough while still being too narrow. The policy check and the existing class definition therefore answer related but different questions.

This is a control policy, not a claim of complete accessibility conformance. The visuals specification makes the same distinction for its chosen card minimum. Names, keyboard operation, contrast, visible focus and error behavior still have their own evidence. [Interface review checklist](interface-review-checklist.md) gathers those areas without turning a size measurement into a blanket result.

## Size sources in the current code

| Element | Source | Existing size behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Card button | `board.css`, `card.css` | Grid tracks from 44px to 88px, square aspect ratio |
| Button, select, input, textarea using `.control` | `control.css` | Minimum height 44px, padding 8px 12px |
| Reproduction summary | `reproduction.css` | Minimum height 44px, padding 12px 16px |
| Deal action row | `controls.css` | Wrapped flex layout, phone buttons grow |
| Reproduction action row | `reproduction.css` | Wrapped flex layout, phone buttons grow |

`game.css` applies `box-sizing: border-box` globally. The declared height constraints therefore include padding and border. Looking only at text line height would underestimate the target, while adding padding to the measured border box would overestimate it.

Cards have `width: 100%`, `aspect-ratio: 1`, zero padding and a `2px` border. Their width comes from the grid track. They do not establish their minimum using the SVG's coordinates or intrinsic artwork size. The current artwork can change shape while the card target remains the same square.

## Why large boards scroll

The inner board calculates a minimum content width from side length, `--card-min` and `--card-gap`. On a sixteen-column board that is 794px before viewport padding and border. A phone cannot display that whole width at once while keeping the current card minimum.

The implementation chooses an internal scroll area. Its `overflow: auto` and `max-width: 100%` allow the board to extend inside a bounded viewport. The outer page stays within the window. This is the reason a sixteen-column board does not respond like a shrunken thumbnail of a four-column board.

A target-size review can therefore encounter two valid observations at once: every card has its intended dimensions, and some cards are outside the current visible portion of the board. Reachability is supplied by scrolling and keyboard movement. [Pointer and touch](pointer-and-touch.md) explains the touch path to the last card; [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) explains arrow access.

A partially clipped card also has a full underlying button box. Clicking the visible part can activate it, after which the current implementation scrolls it fully into view. That behavior does not mean the clipping itself should be measured as the card's intended dimensions. It is an overflow case with a separate focus and pointer timing concern.

## Phone layout affects widths

At `max-width: 599px`, the deal size group fills the row and uses space-between alignment. New Game and Restart receive `flex: 1`. This gives the actions room without hard-coding two button widths. The text and browser control still contribute their intrinsic size constraints.

The reproduction action rows also wrap, with buttons growing on the phone breakpoint. The Board code input has `flex: 1`, a preferred width of `16ch` and `min-width: 0`. The textarea fills its parent and can resize vertically. These choices keep the text tools within the available width rather than making the outer page horizontally scroll.

A visual review at a wide desktop window can miss the consequences of a new wrapper or label. Selectors such as `.controls > button` and `.control-row > button` apply to direct children. If a wrapper changes which element grows, measuring the wrapper rather than the actual button can hide a target-width problem.

The overall content has `16px` page padding and a maximum width of `1120px`. A viewport width is therefore not the same thing as a control's available row width. Panel padding, gaps and borders consume space too. Reading the size policy as a viewport measurement alone would skip the layout where the target actually lives.

## Visible content versus activation area

A native button may contain text, a shape or multiple SVG pieces. In Card, the face SVG and matched check mark are descendants of one button, and the click callback is attached to that button. Their separate geometry does not produce separate tiny controls.

The neutral back is a `12px` span with a rotated border and `aria-hidden="true"`. It is deliberately smaller than the card. Counting its bounds as the input target would describe the drawing rather than the event-handling element. Similarly, the matched check is a state mark, not a separate action with its own click listener.

Focus outlines sit outside the control border and do not add activation area. Hover border changes likewise do not expand the target. Measurements used to assess the policy concern the actual element box; measurements used to assess focus visibility include outline width and offset. The project already has separate helpers for that distinction in `tests/focus-bounds.ts`.

The reproduction summary is another useful case. Its text and disclosure marker occupy only part of a padded native summary element. The element supplies the disclosure interaction. Replacing it with a visually similar small icon could change both target size and semantics; the current source does neither.

## Zoom, density and CSS units

The policy uses CSS pixels. Device pixel ratio affects the mapping to physical pixels, not the DOM geometry reported by `getBoundingClientRect`. A test at device scale 2 can still report a 44px CSS box. Multiplying the bounding-box result by device scale would answer a different question.

The repository's equivalent zoom layout uses a `640x400` viewport with device scale 2. It checks that controls, statistics and the completion summary remain readable and that both small and large boards remain playable. This is useful complementary evidence for a layout that wraps and scrolls rather than simply shrinking every element.

The game does not disable pinch zoom. Card touch handling uses `touch-action: manipulation`, and index.html does not impose a maximum scale. A target remains part of a browser page whose visible scale can change. [Zoom behaviour](../visuals/zoom-behaviour.md) covers the visual contract in more detail.

## Existing evidence and what it establishes

`tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks the default board and control dimensions at `320x640`. It measures `.controls button`, `.controls select` and `.card` boxes and checks minimum width and height. The same file checks large boards at phone and desktop viewports, where the card floor, viewport height and complete focus ring are important.

Those checks establish the existing tested elements at their stated layouts. They do not automatically cover a future control merely because it shares a color or appears next to a tested button. The source selectors and actual bounding box identify the scope of evidence.

For a new feature review, a concise measurement record can identify the viewport, the control's role and name, its width and height and whether it is fully reachable. The record is most useful alongside the rendered layout, because it can reveal that a formally large button is covered by another element or forced beyond the page edge. This is observation of the target in context, not a second numerical policy.

The current game makes many of these checks straightforward by keeping interaction on native DOM elements. There is no canvas hit-map to reconcile with a drawn target. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) explains that architectural advantage, while [Contrast audit](../visuals/contrast-audit.md) and [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) cover other properties that a dimension alone cannot establish.
# Text entry policy

This page records the treatment of person-entered names and distinguishes it from the game's existing code and JSON fields.

Neon Pairs currently asks for a board code and snapshot text, not a player name. There is no name field, group-name store or name rendering component in the source. The name policy below applies when such input is introduced; it does not describe a transformation already applied to the reproduction textarea.

## One name representation

A name can arrive with incidental spaces from typing, pasting or an input method. Keeping several representations of that same entered name would make later display and comparison harder to reason about. Every name a person types is stored and shown after trimming both ends, collapsing each run of inner whitespace to one space and normalizing to NFC. The stored value and visible value therefore describe the same processed name rather than exposing the original draft in one view and a different spelling in another.

The policy is about a person's name. It does not turn all user input into name text, and it does not change the board-code grammar or snapshot serialization. The current fields demonstrate why that distinction matters: significant punctuation and structural whitespace belong to their own formats.

For names, the other checks are documented separately in [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). This page explains representation and input boundaries without duplicating their conditions or error messages.

## Examples of representation

The following examples use quotes only to make surrounding whitespace visible. The quotes are not part of the entered name.

| Entered draft | Displayed and stored form | What changed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `  Mira  ` | `Mira` | Space around the name is removed |
| `Ada   Lovelace` | `Ada Lovelace` | An interior run becomes one separating space |
| `Jean Luc` | `Jean Luc` | Ordinary spacing stays ordinary |
| `Cafe` followed by a combining acute on the e | `Café` | Canonically equivalent text gets a composed representation where available |
| `O'Neil` | `O'Neil` | The apostrophe is retained |

The last example matters because representation cleanup is not an instruction to remove meaningful punctuation or rewrite a person's preferred spelling. The policy does not transliterate scripts, strip accents or convert names to ASCII. Those would be additional transformations beyond what is stated.

NFC addresses canonical equivalence in Unicode text. It is not the compatibility normalization form. Text that merely looks similar is not necessarily canonically equivalent, and this policy does not define visual resemblance as identity. That boundary prevents a representation step from quietly becoming a broad name-matching heuristic.

A name can also contain multiple words. Collapsing a whitespace run does not merge words together; it leaves a separating space. Treating the policy as “delete all whitespace” would change `Ada Lovelace` into a different string and would not implement the stated behavior.

## Drafts and accepted values

A draft is what someone is still editing. A stored value is what an action has accepted. The policy determines the representation of accepted and displayed names, but it does not prescribe that the caret jump after every keystroke or that an input method's partial composition be rewritten while it is active.

That distinction leaves room to implement an editing experience without confusing it with persistence. A reviewer can inspect where a completed entry crosses from local draft state into the feature's model and where the model is rendered. If display uses an old raw draft while storage uses the processed value, the two surfaces no longer have the relationship described above.

The current Reproduction component provides a useful example of draft ownership, though its data is not a name. Its snapshot string lives in local React state and is sent to the decoder on Load snapshot. BoardCodeForm instead reads its native form field at submission. Either storage approach can host an input boundary; the choice of controlled or uncontrolled field does not by itself implement name representation.

No name persistence shape exists in `session/storage.ts`. Its preferences concern size and best move counts. Those fields contain no name preference key, snapshot property or import format.

## Board codes follow a different path

The Board code input is a native text input with `maxLength={32}`, spell checking disabled and autocomplete off. On submission, `use-game.ts` calls `code.trim()` before `parseBoardCode(code)`. That is the only cleanup in that loading path.

The grammar is a version prefix, supported side length and seed separated by hyphens. For example, surrounding spaces around `np1-6-1` are accepted by the control, but an internal space changes the grammar and is rejected. The loader does not collapse arbitrary interior text or repair the seed.

Successful submission replaces the game and refreshes the field from the current code because the input is keyed by generation. Unsuccessful submission preserves the draft. This gives a concrete reference for separating a draft from an accepted representation without applying name transformations to a deal identifier. See [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md).

Board-code parsing is also available as a core function. Calling `parseBoardCode` directly is not the same as passing through the UI loader's trim step. When reading a failure report, the entry point matters. A format parser and an input adapter can have distinct responsibilities without the application guessing what malformed identifiers meant.

## Snapshot text remains structured data

Snapshot JSON has a native textarea length limit and a decoder byte limit. It can include whitespace for readability, and export deliberately produces multiple lines. Its structure is validated before the game is replaced.

Applying name cleanup to the entire JSON draft would conflate two kinds of input. Whitespace can occur between tokens or inside a JSON string, with different meanings. The existing code passes the complete draft to `decodeSnapshot`; it does not first treat it as display prose or a person's name.

The same is true for error preservation. On malformed JSON, the text remains editable and the current game remains present. That behavior supports correction of a structured draft. Accepted names use the normalized representation described above.

[Import safety policy](../sharing/import-safety-policy.md) and [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) explain the current parser and feedback boundaries. Keeping those links close to the input descriptions is more useful than inventing one universal cleanup function for every field on the page.

## Unicode review considerations

Canonical equivalence is easiest to miss when examples are written as visually identical letters. A composed accented character and a base character followed by a combining mark may render alike while having different underlying sequences. A useful representation check includes both forms and inspects the accepted value rather than only its screenshot.

The policy also leaves capitalization alone at this representation step. A comparison operation may have its own policy, but that does not require changing a person's displayed capitalization. Keeping display representation and comparison purpose distinct avoids presenting a comparison key as someone's chosen name.

Likewise, a font's treatment of a character does not change the text stored. A missing glyph, a ligature or a different script's shaping belongs to rendering and typography. The representation policy can be implemented correctly while a layout still needs work to display the name legibly. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) provides the visual context.

The current game has no name-character allowlist or prohibited-name list. Adding one while implementing spacing cleanup would be a separate product decision, not a consequence of Unicode normalization.

## Implementation evidence to look for

There are no name-specific tests in the repository because no name entry has been implemented. The useful evidence for a future implementation would connect its draft, accepted model and displayed text using the cases above. A check confined to an input's current value can miss a storage path that retains an older raw string.

Repeated processing should not progressively change the accepted spelling. The transformations described here have a stable result once applied. If editing, saving and displaying the same accepted name repeatedly removes more content each time, that points to an implementation doing more than the stated representation work.

The current code's strongest relevant lesson is explicit boundaries: BoardCodeForm submits a draft, the controller validates, replacement updates the model, and rendered controls follow that model. Names need their own representation boundary within the feature that introduces them. The present board-code and snapshot controls use their own input boundaries.
# Name length policy

This page defines how the name-length check is interpreted and separates it from native text-field limits.

The current game has no person-name field or name validator. Its existing text limits belong to Board code and Snapshot JSON. They are useful examples of browser entry constraints, but neither is an implementation of the name policy on this page.

## The checked value

The length check concerns the accepted name representation, after the processing described in [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Counting the raw draft instead can produce a different result from counting the value that the feature will store and display. A name has 2 to 20 Unicode code points after normalization. Anything else blocks the action and shows "Use 2 to 20 characters." This check therefore belongs at the point where a draft would become an accepted name, rather than being inferred from the field's apparent width.

The message is the user-facing explanation of this failure. The numerical bounds are inclusive: the endpoints pass, and values outside them fail. The policy does not define an exception for a one-character name, a separate limit for a family name or an alternate bound for another script.

A failure blocks the action that is trying to accept the name. It is not a request to silently cut the entered value to fit. Truncating a longer string would accept a different name and would conceal which action failed. The policy specifies feedback and blocking rather than a repair that guesses the user's intended spelling.

## Code points, code units and visible text

JavaScript string `.length` counts UTF-16 code units. That is not always the number required here. Many characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane occupy two code units but one Unicode code point. For example, `A😀` has three code units and two code points.

A user-perceived symbol can also contain several code points. An emoji sequence joined with a zero-width joiner may look like one symbol while contributing multiple points. A base letter plus a combining mark can be another example, depending on whether canonical composition produces a single point in the accepted form.

The policy chooses code points, not rendered glyph count or grapheme cluster count. A font can draw two code points as one ligature, and an input method can produce a composed-looking sequence. Neither observation changes which unit the check uses. Reviewing only a screenshot cannot establish that the correct unit was counted.

In JavaScript, iterating a string by code point is different from indexing its individual UTF-16 units. `Array.from(value).length` or a spread-based count illustrates that distinction for well-formed text. This is an explanatory example, not a requirement to allocate an array in a particular implementation. The source has no name helper.

## Boundary examples

The examples below assume that the value shown is already in its accepted representation. They illustrate the count, not an additional character allowlist.

| Value | Code-point count | Length result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Empty string | 0 | Fails |
| `A` | 1 | Fails |
| `Al` | 2 | Passes |
| `A😀` | 2 | Passes |
| Twenty ASCII letters | 20 | Passes |
| Twenty-one ASCII letters | 21 | Fails |
| Twenty supplementary-plane symbols | 20 | Passes |

The supplementary-plane example can expose a validator that accidentally uses `.length`: it sees forty code units instead. The opposite mistake is counting a joined visual sequence as one merely because it occupies one displayed cell. A correct boundary check is about the string's code points after representation processing.

“Passes” here means that the length condition is satisfied. It does not imply that an action with other applicable checks is guaranteed to succeed. The [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md) addresses a separate group-level condition without changing the unit used by this check.

## The order is observable

A raw draft may have surrounding or repeated spacing that will not be retained in its accepted form. Counting before the representation step can reject a value that would fit after processing, or accept a value whose later transformations were not what the length helper expected. The policy's ordering avoids having the stored name disagree with the checked name.

A reviewer can follow one candidate from field submission to accepted model and then display. The decisive value is the same one used for the count. An implementation that checks one temporary string but saves a different raw draft has two representations and cannot establish the stated condition simply by having a correctly named length function.

There is no instruction here to run the full action after every individual keystroke. Composition and editing are part of the input experience. The check governs acceptance, while timing of draft feedback is not otherwise specified by the current code or this policy.

## Scope of current evidence

There is no name-length test in the repository. Keyboard and reproduction checks establish native field labels, draft preservation and load outcomes. They do not verify the name count merely because they type strings into controls.

When this policy is implemented, its evidence can name the processed candidate and observed outcome at the boundary. That is enough to distinguish a counting defect from a display problem or another group-level validation failure. The policy stays narrow: one accepted value, one counting unit, one inclusive interval and the stated blocking message.
# Duplicate names policy

This page explains the group-level name comparison policy and the distinctions a reviewer needs when checking it.

The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection.

## Comparison boundary

The group being edited supplies the comparison scope; the draft alone cannot establish whether it repeats an existing entry. The candidate's accepted representation comes from [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Names in one group compare without regard to case, after normalization. A repeat blocks the action and shows "Each name must be different." This lets the same visible spelling with different capitalization be recognized as a repeat without requiring that all displayed names be rewritten in one case.

The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name.

The check concerns names, rather than board positions or face identities. Two cards intentionally share a face, and a replay can intentionally activate the same position more than once. Those repetitions follow their own game rules. A generic “remove duplicates everywhere” helper would not express this policy's subject or scope.

## Display value and comparison value

Case-insensitive comparison does not by itself prescribe changing a name's displayed capitalization. `Mira` and `mira` can compare as the same candidate while the accepted display spelling remains the one chosen by the person who entered it. Showing a lowercased comparison key as the name would conflate two purposes.

A useful implementation trace therefore distinguishes the value displayed, the value accepted into the group and whatever representation is used to compare it. The comparison representation is an internal tool. It is not a new user-visible identifier, a format field or a replacement for the accepted name.

The policy does not specify locale selection or a particular Unicode case-folding API. That matters for names whose case behavior differs across languages or scripts. Name normalization retains diacritics and does not transliterate names. Examples with ordinary Latin letters illustrate the unambiguous case while case behavior across Unicode varies.

The representation step is also not a license to treat all visually similar strings as equal. Latin and Cyrillic lookalikes, differing accents and compatibility characters can resemble one another without being the same processed string. Visual similarity would be a broader identity rule than the policy states.

## Small examples

| Existing accepted name | Candidate | What the example demonstrates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Mira` | `Mira` | A direct repeat |
| `Mira` | `mira` | Capitalization does not distinguish the names |
| `Mira` | `MIRA` | The comparison is not limited to the first letter |
| `Ada Lovelace` | The same name after representation processing | The comparison uses accepted name text |
| `Mira` in another group | `Mira` in this group | The stated scope is the group being edited |

These cases are illustrations of the policy rather than a complete Unicode test corpus. They also do not decide length validity; [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) covers that independent check. A candidate can satisfy length and still repeat an existing name.

A group with several entries can expose a bug that a two-entry example misses. If only the immediately preceding name is checked, a repeat of the first entry can slip through after a different middle entry. The policy speaks about the group, so the relevant evidence is membership across that group rather than adjacency in the rendered form.

## Blocking has a concrete meaning

A repeated candidate does not become an accepted additional name as part of the failed action. The exact feedback above explains why acceptance stopped. Automatically adding a suffix, changing capitalization or deleting one of the existing names would implement a different outcome from the one stated.

This policy does not decide which error wins when several checks fail at once. It also does not add live validation on every keystroke, a suggestion picker or a search across previous games. Those are separate interaction choices, and none is present in the source.

The current reproduction handlers demonstrate an explicit acceptance boundary: parse first, replace only on success, otherwise publish a notice. A name feature can be reviewed with the same question—where does a candidate become accepted?—without reusing the board parser or claiming that load errors are name errors. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) provides the current feedback mechanics.

## Evidence a reviewer can assess

Because no name feature exists, the existing tests do not establish this policy. A screenshot containing distinct visible names would be weak evidence even for a future feature: the comparison bug might only appear on submission, on an edit or after a change in capitalization.

Useful examples include an exact repeat, a case-only repeat, a repeat that is not adjacent in the displayed list and a different accepted name. An edit scenario reveals whether the current entry is being confused with another entry. A separate-group example reveals whether an implementation accidentally enforces a broader scope than the policy states.

For a defect report, the accepted group values, candidate value, action and observed message make the comparison reproducible. Display order can be recorded as context, but it does not define identity. The policy stays about equality within the group, and its representation and length dependencies remain in their own linked pages.
# Announcements policy

This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering.

The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards.

## Publication point

`Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature.

The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source.

Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader.

## Session data behind the paragraph

The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `<span key={session.announcement}>{session.feedback}</span>`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text.

The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it.

A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`.

## Turn results

`activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal.

After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications.

| Result | Text produced by the session |
| --- | --- |
| First matched pair | `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` |
| Later nonfinal pair | `Pair found. M pairs matched.` |
| Mismatch | `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` |
| Winning pair | `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.` |

Here `M` and `N` are replaced with the actual counts, and `time` is the output of `formatElapsed`. The singular branch is based on `game.matched.length === 2`. The final branch takes precedence over the nonfinal pair count.

A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. [Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) follows those two sources in a complete game.

## Consecutive identical results

Two misses in a row produce the same sentence. Updating only a string state can leave the DOM text unchanged, which gives no new mutation for the second event. The keyed span avoids relying on a different visible sentence to distinguish them.

The current sequence is concrete. Initial feedback is empty. Revealing index 0 on `np1-4-1` changes selection to `one` without publishing. Revealing index 1 produces a mismatch and advances the event identity. After the interval closes, choosing those two indices again produces the same text with a later identity.

The counter advances once for each resolved attempt in that sequence, not once for each card action or timer update. A third activation during the mismatch is ignored by the game and leaves the event unchanged. The same is true of a repeated activation on the first revealed card.

There is no temporary blanking timeout between identical results. The implementation does not clear text, wait a guessed number of milliseconds and restore it. That avoids adding announcement timing to the game clock or introducing a second lifecycle that can outlive a replacement game.

## Changes that stay quiet

`tickSession` advances the game and returns a new session with that game, leaving feedback and announcement fields intact. Mismatch closure is part of this advancement. It does not publish a new “cards closed” result. The earlier mismatch sentence already told the player that closure would follow a short pause.

Arrow movement is local board focus state. It does not call the session feedback path. Clock renders update Time in GameStatus, while card memoization prevents unchanged cards from rendering again. Neither operation is a new turn result.

New Game and Restart call `replaceGame` with `imported: false`. That replacement clears the prior feedback and load notice while keeping the announcement number. A successful board-code load follows the same replacement path. These operations clear old context; the current source does not add a success sentence for a board-code load.

Clearing text is still a DOM change and may appear in a mutation trace as an empty result. It is different from republishing a turn sentence. The accessibility journey's expected record includes the new-game clearing event, so a raw count of every mutation is not a substitute for reading what each event contains.

## Load outcomes share the publication path

The controller's `notice(feedback)` helper assigns both `feedback` and `loadNotice`, then increments `announcement`. Invalid Board code publishes `Invalid board code.`; invalid Snapshot JSON publishes `Invalid snapshot.`. Repeating the same invalid submission is a new load attempt and advances the identity again.

For valid snapshot import, `replaceGame(..., true)` increments the identity and publishes either `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` or `Loaded completed snapshot.`. The former corresponds to a paused unfinished game, the latter to completed progress. Valid board-code loading does not use the imported-snapshot branch.

Reproduction also renders `loadNotice` in its ordinary paragraph with id `load-notice`. The load buttons reference it through `aria-describedby`. That keeps the outcome visible beside the text tools and associates the description with their actions without creating another event publisher in that panel.

Resume clears feedback and loadNotice without increasing the event identity. It also transfers focus to the board before its button disappears. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) and [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) describe those effects independently of event publication.

## Completion and persistent reading

GameStatus shows a completion paragraph whenever `isWon(game)` is true. A newly won game can give it the celebration class; an imported completed game shows it statically. That paragraph is persistent reading content containing the final moves and time.

The winning turn's feedback already contains the match and win in one result. The status paragraph does not need to separately announce a matched pair, then publish a second completion sentence. This avoids having two updates compete at the most significant turn in the game.

A completed snapshot instead publishes its load outcome, because import is the event that just occurred. The game is visibly complete, but no new card match happened. This distinction preserves a useful account of what the user actually did.

## Automated evidence

`session.test.ts` checks that first reveal, mismatch closure and repeated mismatch events affect announcement identity as expected. It also checks import outcomes and completion transitions without involving the browser.

`tests/announcements.e2e.test.ts` observes DOM mutations in the status paragraph. It resolves a mismatch, moves focus, runs the mismatch interval and repeats the same attempt. The expected result history contains the mismatch sentence once for each resolved turn, with no extra result from movement or closure.

The same test submits each snapshot load kind and each invalid-load kind twice, checking the publication history and the visible load notice. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` checks that the result remains beside the board during large-phone play and that the reproduction panel has no competing result role.

The accessibility journey reads Chromium's tree for the polite and atomic properties and the result text at each turn. That establishes exposure in the tested runtime. Spoken scheduling and verbalization are assessed in user acceptance. The repository records spoken review as user acceptance.

## Diagnosing a repeated or missing result

A missing second identical result suggests checking event identity before changing the sentence. A repeated result on every clock tick suggests checking whether routine advancement touches the publication fields. A load notice visible near the textarea but absent from event output suggests checking whether the controller used `notice` or only changed local text.

For a report, the useful sequence is the action, feedback string, announcement number and observed mutations. That evidence can show whether the session failed to publish, React had no relevant change or the browser exposed the expected update but a spoken review behaved differently. The policy gives a single publication boundary; diagnosis follows it from the event to the paragraph rather than adding more announcers around the page.
# Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

There is no result table in the current UI. `GameStatus.tsx` displays four properties of a single game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons. None of those structures is evidence that ordered records have already been implemented.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.

The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.

The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen.

[Status bar](status-bar.md) documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.

## Why the card board is not a table

Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.

The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.

There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.

## What the caption contributes

An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.

The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.

A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.

## Column relationships and reading order

The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure.

A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.

Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.

## Narrow layouts and long values

The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.

There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.

Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) and [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.

The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) provides the wider review context.
